9A

New knowledgeHow is work calculated?

Work

Work is the amount of energy transferred by a force from one object or system to another.

Work is a scalar quantity.

The amount of work done on an object can be calculated by multiplying the displacement by the force that is applied parallel to the direction of displacement.

Imagine a box being pulled along a frictionless floor as shown below This can be expressed mathematically as follows. W=Fscos⁡θW = Fs\cos\thetaW=Fscosθ Although work is a scalar quantity, it can still be positive or negative because the energy can be given to an object or taken away from an object.

Unlabelled diagram (box pulled at angle) Imagine a box being pulled along a frictionless floor as shown below
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 73
9A

New knowledgeHow is work calculated?

Work

Take a bowling ball, for example: while your hand is in contact with the bowling ball, energy is being given to the ball.

Once the ball has been released by your hand, a small rolling friction force acts on the ball in the opposite direction to its motion.

Therefore, the work done can be considered negative.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 74
9A

New knowledgeWhen a force performs no work

Work

It is possible to apply a constant force on an object and not transfer any energy to the object.

For example, if you hold an object in a fixed position, you are applying a constant force on the object.

You can feel the effort of holding the object, but no energy is being transferred to it.

This is because there is no displacement of the object and, as a result of W=Fscos⁡θW = Fs\cos\thetaW=Fscosθ, since the displacement is zero the work is also zero.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 75
9A

New knowledgeForce–distance graphs

Work

The work done can also be determined by analysing a force–distance graph.

A force–distance graph displays force component on the y-axis and distance on the x-axis, as shown in the following diagram.

The work done can be determined by calculating the area under the graph.

To calculate the work done in the above diagram above, y force would have to be multiplied by x distance; as the force is being multiplied by the distance, the product will always be the work done in joules.

Figure 9A–5 Example of a force-distance graph with a constant force y applied over a distance x.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 96

A man pushes a box of mass 46 kg horizontally along the ground with a force of 500 N. The box encounters a frictional force of 50 N. Calculate the amount of work done on the box to push it 32 m.
a Calculate the work done on the box by the pushing force.
b Calculate the work done against the box by the friction force.
c Calculate the energy given to the box.
Key idea · WorkW=Fscos⁡θW = Fs\cos\thetaW=Fscosθ

Working

a Wpush=Fpushscos⁡θ=(500)(32)cos⁡0∘=16 000 JW_{\text{push}} = F_{\text{push}}s\cos\theta = (500)(32)\cos 0^\circ = 16\,000\ \text{J}Wpush​=Fpush​scosθ=(500)(32)cos0∘=16000 J
b Wfriction=Ffrictionscos⁡θ=(50)(32)cos⁡180∘=−1600 JW_{\text{friction}} = F_{\text{friction}}s\cos\theta = (50)(32)\cos 180^\circ = -1600\ \text{J}Wfriction​=Ffriction​scosθ=(50)(32)cos180∘=−1600 J
c Wtotal=Wpush+Wfriction=(16 000)+(−1600)=14 400 JW_{\text{total}} = W_{\text{push}} + W_{\text{friction}} = (16\,000) + (-1600) = 14\,400\ \text{J}Wtotal​=Wpush​+Wfriction​=(16000)+(−1600)=14400 J
a 16 000 J; b −1600 J; c 14 400 J

We doWork from force–distance graph

Work
A broken-down car is pushed with a force of 0.95 kN in the direction of displacement for 20 m. The person who is pushing the car then tires and their force in the direction of displacement reduces at a constant rate to zero over the next 10 m. A force–distance graph of this situation is shown on the right. Calculate the work done by the person pushing the car.
Key idea · WorkW=Fscos⁡θW = Fs\cos\thetaW=Fscosθ

Working

The work done is the area under the graph, this graph would need to be broken up into a rectangle and a triangle as shown. (Note: kN must be converted into N.)
total area = total work
=(0.95×103×20)+(12×0.95×103×10)= (0.95\times10^{3}\times20) + \left(\frac{1}{2}\times0.95\times10^{3}\times10\right)=(0.95×103×20)+(21​×0.95×103×10)
=2.38×104 J= 2.38\times10^{4}\ \text{J}=2.38×104 J
2.38×1042.38\times10^{4}2.38×104 J

A tugboat is attached to a large ship via a rope that pulls in the same direction as the direction that the boat is moving. The graph displaying how the tugboat pulls on the ship as a function of the distance travelled is displayed below.

Working

a Wfirst 30 m=(100×103)(26)+(100+130)×1032(4)W_{\text{first 30 m}} = (100\times10^{3})(26) + \frac{(100+130)\times10^{3}}{2}(4)Wfirst 30 m​=(100×103)(26)+2(100+130)×103​(4)

=2.65×106 J= 2.65\times10^{6}\ \text{J}=2.65×106 J
The work done in the first 30 m is greater.
b The work is given by W=Fscos⁡θW = Fs\cos\thetaW=Fscosθ, where the cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ calculates the force is parallel to the direction of displacement if the rope were pulling at an angle, cos⁡θ<1\cos\theta < 1cosθ<1, giving a smaller value than the actual pulling force. This means that the pulling force would need to be increased to keep the amount of work constant.
